Chloé Zhao's third feature Nomadland is a slow-burning drama about a widowed nomad traveling the American West in the wake of the 2007 financial crisis that decimated her small town. Culled from the 2017 book of the same name, Zhao's adaptation is a somber affair built entirely on the reflections of a forgotten underclass piecing together what remains of their arduous lives. This elegy to loss is slightly effecting in its exploration of working class peril, but remains an aimless dramatization of firsthand accounts of a beleaguered lifestyle. In comparison to prior works of the same ilk (Lean on Pete, Leave No Trace, Winter's Bone), Nomadland is a lightweight document that is as undemanding as it is depressingly lethargic.

Paired with a singular vision from director Chloe Zhao, a brilliant performance by Frances McDormand, and stunning cinematography including many wide shots that look glorious in IMAX, #Nomadland is a heartwarming story of a journey of one woman across America. Final score: 5/5.

One of this year's clear award contenders, the Chloé Zhao written, directed and edited Nomadland is a quiet elegy on freedom and time with loud emotional resonance. The yet again flawless Frances McDormand, likely to get a third Oscar for this role, is Fern, a woman who has lost everything, including her husband and her home in the aftermath of 2008's Great Recession and is now forced to roam the United States in her RV, working what she can, where she can, meeting many other modern day nomads down the road. On her travels, she discovers some truths about the self exactly as we do. Once asked whether she's homeless, Fern responds "I'm houseless. Not the same thing, right?".

Elevated even higher by a beautifully melancholic score, Zhao's naturalistic and deeply personal shots transport us not only in the middle of the unique American plains, but also in a particular space of mind that makes you forget the film's initial question of "What do you do when the world fails you?" and gives you entirely different food for thought. It present life not as cruel or unfair, but as a raw, unfiltered journey full of stories and experiences, circular by definition. I believe Zhao's brilliance and her deep understanding in the film's vision can be seen in the simple, yet extraordinary fact that Nomadland's sequences could have been edited in almost any order and it would have worked just as fine. As a downside to this, the direction sometimes falls into the trap of slight self indulgence, but McDormand's committed performance always seems to ground the film back to the realm of realism.

Nomadland is a startlingly beautiful film of quiet humanity and generous community. It is natural to a degree that will make you feel deeply about the characters depicted. A film of enormous depth and honesty. It tells the story of Fern, a middle aged woman living and working in a small town in Nevada. The gypsum plant that supports the town closes and the town effectively becomes a ghost town. Soon after her husband dies, so she sells up buys a van and looks for seasonal work. Firstly at an Amazon centre before Christmas. It is there that she is told of 'nomadland', a community in Arizona that people visit that live the 'nomad' way of life. Frances McDormand is simply brilliant as Fern, such a naturalistic actor, she immerses herself in each and every scene. But the nomads in the film are actually the people who live this life on the road and are non actors. It lends an authenticity to the film that is impressive to say the least. The community are not portrayed as desperate or losers but simply as people who society forgot about and are simply trying to survive with the help of friends. Fern embraces this lifestyle travelling across many states taking seasonal jobs whilst living in her van. This superb film is overflowing with pathos and humanity, a gentle and kind portrait of people living and surviving. Chloe Zhao is a serious talent, her direction is first class and she shows a real empathy with all aspects of humanity. Using the natural landscapes of states like South Dakota, Arizona and Wyoming the film is a joy to watch too with a delicate score by Ludovico Einaldi to enhance the quiet drama. The film moves slowly but I never once felt it needed a faster pace. It is often about conversations and listening, something I love in films. This film is profound and glorious. One of the best films of 2020.

A beautifully shot and earnestly acted film about living on the road, Nomadland could easily have been a Terrence Malickesque arthouse flick that spent all its time staring at things without having anything interesting to say about them. Fortunately, director/screenwriter Chloé Zhao wisely keeps scenes at a reasonable length and avoids lingering shots, and as a result the runtime is kept relatively short, and things happen at a much more realistic pace. There were a few montage-like shots that I felt were unnecessary, especially since all of them seem to have the same piece of piano music played over them, but for the most part the movie's eye in in the right place. Centring around a stripped-down, raw performance by Frances McDormand, it focuses on those who were affect by this century's recession, and how many people it left destitute and directionless. Certain members of the cast and crew actually lived in vans throughout production to get a feel for that particular way of life, and that definitely comes through onscreen. It often feels like the characters are simply floating from place to place, lost in their own world with no idea of where they're truly going. It's very much a free-spirited film, unbound by conventional film structure, feeling more like a dream than a story. It's a film I know will not be to everyone's tastes. The premise certainly suggests it'll be full of long stares and endless driving through the wilderness, but the movie eschews superfluous landscape shots and pretentious philosophizing and instead focuses on a group of individuals united by circumstance, and shows how they have come to deal with it in their own way. More than anything, it's about the complexities of human life. It can be funny, it can be heart-warming, it can be tragic. Not a film destined for box office success, but it one that will hopefully to stick in the public conscience for years to come.

Nomadland is exactly what the trailer promises-a slow moving study of a woman dealing with a life changing crisis just when she thought she was safe . Fern isn't an easy character to understand. At first it was hard to even like Fern. She certainly is a woman of strong will and she's resilient and she's not afraid of tough manual labor. At first I sort of rejected the character as not real enough. She's not crying over her loss. There's no self pity of her circumstances. That made it a little difficult to embrace her as at first. (But later we learn her journey had already started long before we joined her. So the stage of self-pity and crying may have long passed). 

Later though when I was home thinking about it I realized that just because a character ( male or female) doesn't show a tender side doesn't mean she or he isn't real. Yes there are a lot of Ferns out there chugging along trying to survive. And just the juxtaposition of the name Fern-a delicate house plant - made me think.

Frances McDormand has few lines and relies on just being physically present and does a wonderful job doing just that. The important dialogue belongs to the people see meets along the way in Nomadland. Some are broke, some have money, some are running away and some are running towards something.  Each nomad has a story that's just as interesting as the last and they are the ones that I am glad Zhao choose to focus on. It's a study of America that could be dropped in any period of it's history.

This inside look at a little-known community and culture is engaging for about the first two-thirds, but, in the end run, it begins to grow tiresome, leaving viewers wondering when and how it will ever end. Director Chloe Zhao's third feature offering is a notable improvement over her first two outings, but she still needs to refine her craft further to produce the kind of masterpiece she's likely capable of. "Nomadland" is a big step in that direction, serving up a heartfelt tale about the American nomadic community and its unconventional followers' love of the freedom it affords, set against the beauty of the country's landscape, depicted here through stunningly gorgeous cinematography. However, the inherent meandering of the protagonist ultimately gets taken a little too far in the film's narrative and could have been trimmed without losing anything. The much-heralded performance of Frances McDormand is adequate but far from the kind of stellar work she's capable of, probably due to the understated nature of her character, a casting decision that maybe should have been reevaluated before filming began. While I can honestly say I liked this film, I can also honestly say that I didn't love it, either. Maybe the fourth time will be the charm for Ms. Zhao.

This was a difficult move to rate. As a film, it is absolutely brilliant in every aspect. McDormand gives a tour de force performance. The cinematography and musical score are both as close to perfection as they could be. The story is beautiful and touching. But therein lies the problem. The story, a clear indictment of everything that is wrong in the US and the inequalities resulting from unbridled capitalism and plutocratic rule, is just too much on the nice side of prettied up by Hollywood for the suburban and urban elite. While there are many aspects of the nomad life that ring true, and clearly show some effort to be honest, it glosses over way too much of the everyday nitty gritty and the harsh realities. As if work at an Amazon facility were so pleasant. As if working on a sugar beet harvest involved just those few moments shown rather than weeks of constant body-draining effort. As if Fern would really betray her values and take the money from her sister. Sadly, the film serves most to soothe the guilt of the self-proclaimed woke.

NOMADLAND stars Frances McDormand as Fern, a widower nearing retirement who can't make ends meet by taking early social security. She lived in Empire, Nevada with her husband until 2011, where the film begins, until his death and the closing of the plant. Fern works odd end and seasonal jobs while traveling to support herself. She lives in her van and travels around the country from Nevada, to Arizona, to South Dakota, and California. At first, with this being so close to the market collapse of 2008, the viewer may believe this is a film dealing with classism in America and the capitalistic exploitation of its workers; however, that notion is quickly dispelled as we follow Fern and her friends from community to community. It's actually a very touching tale about these communities that society has forgotten about. It's very much a commune where individuals band together like family members, are welcomed and invited, and help each other survive. It also explores the hurdles some of these individuals must overcome in order to do the most mundane of tasks, like getting a flat tire fixed and other inconveniences that we take for granted but is a real struggle for them. McDormand brings a lot of life to Fern and while her performance does stand out, it isn't her best work and even if she's nominated for an Oscar, I'd be surprised if she won for this performance. Other than that, there's nothing much else here.

From psychology, we know that "nomadism" is a pathological tendency for some to wander from location to location often giving rise to instability and in severe cases disorientation. In an attempt to escape the responsibilities accompanying stressful situations, some of us succumb to itinerant lifestyles. Of course, this suggests the dark side of a Chloe Zhao's new film, Nomadland, that chooses to ignore the main character's PTSD (she left Empire, a Colorado mining town that dies, and takes her husband Bo with it) only to replace it with some hankering for independence and adventure.  For this reason, many viewers will find Nomadland a bad trip. In the last act of the film, main character Fern (stoically played by Frances McDormand) dodges the opportunity to make a new life for herself in an idyllic suburban estate owned by her sister. A magnanimous friend Dave (David Strathairn) wants her to stay but she rejects him for a call to the wild. So, audiences are faced with the question, is Fern's travelling a future quest or is she starving for the past? Today, with the pandemic, we are living in some pretty tough times, times that make self-reliance, individualism, and isolation more fashionable. For me, I'd rather die with a loved one next to my bed, than in some Arizona desert with a van that refuses to start.

Don't expect to be on the edge of your seat with excitement or even thoroughly entertained, because that's not what the film is and that's not what it's supposed to be. It's a slow, quiet, look behind the curtain that isn't driven by a central plot, but rather by its tone. Frances McDormand is Endearing as a Wandering Nomad Displaced by the American Recession: "Nomadland," directed by Chloé Zhao ("The Rider"), written by Zhao, based on the book by Jessica Bruder, follows the story of Fern, played by the once again brilliant, 2-time Oscar-winner, Frances McDormand, a woman forced to become a Nomad after the losses of her job in 2011 at a shut down factory in Nevada, her home, death of her husband and the town she lived in wiped off the map, all painful misfortunes, the results of the American Recession. Fern buys a van, which she customizes as her new home, and wanders the West in a constant search for work, including taking a seasonal job with other Nomads boxing packages at a large Amazon distribution center. The beauty in Chloé Zhao's direction is her ability to play on realism by mixing actors in the film with non-actors who manage to give equally gritty performances. Joshua James Richards, Zhao's Cinematographer, is truly an artist, capturing the breathtaking landscape of the American West, using his camera to paint an alluring palette of the stark Arizona desert, ominous mountains, long, winding, cold and lonely roads, powerful Pacific coastline, the Redwood Forest and glorious sunrises and sunsets.

Frances McDormand is pretty much always fantastic and fierce and convincing and all-around amazing. If she's featured or starring in a film, that's a "must see" for me, because she's also pretty choosy about her projects. And all the buzz around NOMADLAND really had me very excited to see it. I didn't know too much about it, but I did know that it would feature McDormand as a "nomad", essentially a person not living in a house but moving around the country, following low-paying jobs wherever they can be found (mostly seasonal work) and living out of an RV, van or car. A study of life on the fringes of American life. Not exactly "homeless" but "house-less." A loose-knit society, all struggling to make it, and all helping each other where they can.

And in many ways, that is the movie we get. Writer/director Chloe Zhao has taken a nearly documentarian's approach to the film. It is indeed scripted, and aside from McDormand, also features the always enjoyable David Strathairn. But most of the rest of the cast are actual nomads playing, essentially, versions of themselves. It all feels very much filmed on location at these encampments, including the very famous gatherings in Quartzite, AZ. McDormand's widow Fern, forced to leave the town that essentially evaporated with the closing of the gypsum factory that was its only reason to exist, learns about this nomadic existence pretty much as the viewer does. We see the hardships of a cramped van (she can't even stretch out to full length in her bed), the hard-scrabble existence, the campfires and camaraderie, and underlying it all is the gift of a closeness to the beauty of our land and also the "curse" of knowing just how close to the edge of existence this life is. It is clearly a mixed blessing in every sense of the phrase.

My favorite part of the film may have been simply enjoying the lingering shots of some amazing American vistas, whether the sparseness of Nevada away from the cities, the beauty of the South Dakota Badlands or the roiling character of the California coast away from the beaches and tourists. All this land we have set aside for the enjoyment of our citizens is also the only true way these nomads are able to live the life they do. The beauty offers the comforts of this life.

The film itself has virtually no plot. Although there are little emotional payoffs throughout, it is a film of brief stories and images. Various folks Fern meets share small moments of their lives (an elderly lady, dying of cancer, tells Fern of the time she came upon a cliff full of thousands of swallows and how lucky she is to have seen something like that. Moments like that are when the film really gets you. It's sneaky like that). We learn a little bit about Fern throughout the film, but McDormand never makes it easy for us to get close to Fern. She holds others at arms length, and although she is a very kind person, she certainly has built an armor for herself. Towards the end of the film a few things happen that sort of resemble a plot, but in many ways, we pretty much know how things will resolve during these moments. The film's plot has few surprises; yet the people we meet and the conversations we listen in on constantly surprise.

Frankly, it's a movie that helps us see a group of people we might normally not give much notice to. They ARE on the fringes, but they are not out of touch. They care for each other in ways that could teach much of the rest of society a lesson. In many ways, the film is about small kindnesses. How sharing a cigarette lighter can be a huge act of kindness that will be remembered months later.

There are many things to enjoy and feel in NOMADLAND. But despite all the glowing things I mention above, I still didn't quite love the film. The pace is VERY slow, but not to the point of being boring. I think perhaps it was the juxtaposition between traditional film, with real actors like McDormand speaking character dialogue and having little plot-like things to deal with, and the more documentary style wherein real people tell their stories or engage in moments of dialogue in the slightly awkward way any of us who don't act in front of a camera would likely have. There are many things to admire about Zhao's approach (and I respect the idea of having these nomads speak for themselves), but for me, it doesn't quite work. It made me aware too often that I was watching a film that was experimenting with style and form. At times, images and incidents flowed over me in a beautiful way and at others, I was jarred with "oh hey, this actor is just a real person trying to handle dialogue."

Having said that, the film is still well worth watching. McDormand is quietly gripping and the beauty of the land and the presentation of a nearly unknown way of life is very worthwhile to see.

An atmospheric indie film to which Chloé Zhao has lent a great deal of down-to-earthness, humanity and poetics with her sensitivity in the director's chair and which is considered a hot contender for this year's Oscar race. Nomadland is a character study of the suddenly "houseless" Fern, who tries to adapt to her new life as a nomad as best she can after the death of her husband. On the almost documentary-like followed journey in her van, Fern meets people with different personalities who help her in her new world.  

The centre of the film throughout the entire running time is clearly protagonist Fern, played by two-time Oscar winner Frances McDormand. She undergoes all kinds of setbacks and always carries around an inner conflict. She could do better, but wants to take the challenge on herself with all her might. McDormand embodies the basic mood of the film and tells the story of many: she is a victim of the glaring class differences and capitalist overweight in the USA. In the process, she works her fingers to the bone, is constantly on the lookout for new jobs and means well for people. She illustrates what the new situation triggers in her character and how she keeps her head above water. Fern goes hand in hand with the mood of the film: she is unobtrusive, subtle and has a lot of depth. This role is arguably the most important in McDormand's glorious career so far because she represents a group of people who are not seen. The actress lived in a van on a campsite for a few months before the start of filming herself and got acquainted with this kind of life. David Strathairn, as Fern's good friend Dave, is also very important to the protagonist's journey. He makes her conflicted by his obvious intentions and lets us experience the interpersonal component first hand. This comes across in almost every scene in the film, despite the clear main character. The other characters are real-life people, which brings an enormous amount of closeness and authenticity to the film.

McDormand carries the plot of the film brilliantly on her shoulders, but the real heroine of Nomadland is its director. You can tell from start to finish that Chloé Zhao cares deeply about this subject matter. She has turned a low-budget independent film into a technical masterpiece against which every action film with elaborate special effects falls short. The cinematography captures lengthy and beautiful shots of the landscape, making the film's actually dreary setting seem colourful and idyllic. The music by Ludovico Einaudi is softly and empathetically composed, making Fern's rides in the van meaningful. Zhao has put together a film that takes its time, but where all the cinematic elements become one big whole. As a result, Nomadland does not create seas of tears despite the sadness of its subject, but a cinematic masterpiece whose basic idea is always present and sticks with one.

The duality of 'Nomadland' is what impacts me the most. Although (the reliably-captivating) Frances McDormand's experience is the anchor, Chloe Zhao populates the film with as many perspectives as possible to emphasize that true liberation and spiritual peace of mind are entirely different notions based on who's answering. There's an unshakable beauty to that.

Literally everything about this film can be described with the word "beautiful". The acting, the direction, the writing, the cinematography, the characters, the story, the atmosphere, the documentary-like feel, the warm-hearted tone, and the themes of freedom, materialism, wealth, and, perhaps most prominently, America itself. Director/writer/editor Chloe Zhao refines the talent she showed in The Rider with an elegant kind of simplicity that guides viewers along a quiet cinematic journey, one that doesn't talk down to its audience without ever being shallow or pretentious. Her command over visual and narrative craft is simply amazing here, emphasizing minimalist filmmaking to maximize emotional impact. Frances McDormand gives one of the best performances of her career and definitely one of her more restrained ones, especially compared to her righteously furious Oscar-winning performance in Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. The supporting cast is surprisingly strong as well, with David Strahairn, Swankie, Linda May, and Bob Wells all turning in impressively poignant and entertaining performances, feats that are made particularly commendable when the latter three are real-life nomads rather than professional actors. The cinematography is absolutely gorgeous and stunning and at times truly jaw-dropping, often times evoking Emmanuel Lubezki's incredible work on The Revenant in its frequent, almost loving shots of nature and the people that inhabit it. Like I said at the start of this review, Nomadland is an utterly beautiful film, perfectly embodying the American spirit in a respectful and universally relatable manner. The best film of 2020.

"Nomadland" is a direct and honest film that resonates because of the way it simply allows itself to be and for the way it portrays a lifestyle that simply is. As the name indicates, it is about living as a nomad, which, in this day and age, can involve driving and parking from one place to another; taking various odd jobs to make ends meet; learning new skills we might have assumed were lost to automation or performed by someone other than ourselves; making new friends the old-fashioned way, which is to say in person; rationing resources; and repeating this cycle throughout the year in order to survive. A nomadic life can be both disheartening and joyous, but then again, can't every life?

What initially draws us into this film's raw and organic world is its teaching us about nomadism, which, for most viewers (just as it did for me), will render both impressive and eye-opening, not to mention scary and exciting. I felt enlightened as the film taught me just a few of the things it takes to subsist as a modern-day nomad, even though all humans used lived this way millions of years ago.

It may seem like common knowledge, but life as a wanderer isn't easy. Supplies can be limited; money can be tight; temperatures can drop; vehicles can break down; tires can get flats; feelings of isolation and desolation can be commonplace (as can feeling smothered); and one can easily get desperate and angry during hard times.

"Nomadland" simply introducing us to this way of life, which is often handled by the real-life nomads who appear in the film, alone makes it valuable and, in many ways, fascinating. But what keeps us engaged is how the film regards its subject and people with such balance and straightforwardness. It neither promotes nor discourages nomadism but rather tells an observant and essentially impartial story that seeks to show and tell us about the itinerant lifestyle so that we might learn from it and reflect upon it. It's rare for a film to be so naturally neutral yet so detailed and perceptive.

Of course, our instincts and experiences with Hollywood narratives tell us there should be more to it, that there must be a catch. There isn't. Writer-director Chloé Zhao gently and unaffectedly informs us of the characters and their ways of life through calming imagery, patience and genuine human behavior. Her camera makes it a point not to be intrusive, and yet it she isn't trying to be rebellious by not letting her screenplay, based on Jessica Bruder's non-fiction book, "Nomadland: Surviving America in the Twenty-First Century," succumb to contrived plot developments or trite messages. On the contrary, it's as if conventions or clichés of any kind never even entered Zhao's purview. Like the nomads we encounter in the film, Zhao simply wants to pass on knowledge so we can grow from it.

The story opens on a somber note. It's 2011 and the city of Empire, Nevada has recently collapsed under economic hardship. Empire is where the film's heroine, Fern (Frances McDormand), and her late husband, Bo, lived and worked most of their adult lives, but in the wake of US Gypsum shutting down its sheetrock plant, the city became nothing short of a ghost town and its lone zip code was discontinued. Fern, who doesn't have children, has no choice but to empty her storage locker and hit the road in her run-down, white conversion van. From here on out, her van is where she'll eat, sleep, uses the facilities, and do her best to conserve space. "I'm not homeless," she tells friends who ask her to come live with them, "I'm houseless."

Like many nomads, Fern adapts and moves around the country according to the seasons, from Arizona to South Dakota. She finds work wherever she can, including an Amazon fulfillment center, national parks, and fast food restaurants. She buys and sells only the essentials, often from fellow travelers, and parks her van wherever she's allowed and can remain the most inconspicuous. 

One of the interesting things about Fern as a character is we feel for her but we don't necessarily feel sorry for her. Even though she's on the road, she has the option to live with others, be they friends, her sister Dolly (Melissa Smith) and brother-in-law George (Warren Keith), or another itinerant she meets at different times along the road named Dave (David Strathairn), who expresses a romantic interest.

But settling down and being beholden to others, either financially or emotionally, are burdens Fern no longer wants to bear. We suspect her husband's death has made her cautious about getting too close to people, but we also take her for a strong, independent woman who can be stubborn and is a loner at heart. Fern is in her mid-60s and feels the urge to explore, even if that means being broke and by herself.

As one of the film's producers, McDormand has said she had her heart set on realizing this project for years and both her and Zhao's love and fascination for the material are felt throughout (in preparation for filming, the two navigated the country in vans for months, just as Fern does). In many ways, McDormand is simply playing herself on-screen, having told her real-life husband (filmmaker Joel Cohen) that when she turned 65, she wanted to change her name to Fern and hit the road in her RV. But whether or not McDormand actually had these ambitions is beside the point. What matters is she still gives her stalwart character a spirit, depth and curiosity that make her unique and identifiable. McDormand so fitting and dedicated that we've no reason to think of anyone else in the role; she is Fern and she brings us along on her journey.

However, this isn't to say she invited us. In fact, Fern makes it clear she doesn't always want to be living this way. With all its logistical hurdles, emotional upheavals, and moments of loneliness and self-doubt, living as a nomad can make one prone to pain, suffering and heartache. But it can also spur many pleasures, close friendships, and an appreciation for things we often take for granted, such as the outdoors, the night sky, a comfortable chair, and bestowing knowledge onto others.

In other words, nomadic living is still living, just a different kind than most of us are used to. This notion, I think, ties into the film's greater message, which is that nomadism is neither better nor worse than a more traditional, settled existence. Each has their pluses and minuses but it's important we recognize both as worthy in their own right and appreciate that life, in any sense, is precious and transitory, so we should make the most of it.

"Nomadland" isn't biased, cynical or pushy. Fern faces hard times just like the rest of us but the film isn't interested in how she got to where she is, only how she handles her present situation. It doesn't want to polarize us over such heavy topics as capitalism or corporate malfeasance  (the screenplay mentions these but only minimally). Instead, it focuses on the idea that no matter what life tosses our way, we should be able to rely on others and ourselves to be open-minded and offer help and guidance to navigate it as best we can.

In addition to having a refreshing, apolitical agenda, "Nomadland" serves as a consummate cinematic experience. Joshua James Richards' cinematography, Ludovico Einaudi's music (featuring pieces taken from previously recorded albums), and Zhao's editing collectively put us in a state of tranquility. The film isn't slow so much as it's not in a hurry and watching and listening to  it, we get the impression Zhao wanted us to be able to either close our eyes or plug our ears and still experience moments of great sensation. Through stunning wide and long shots of rich, infinite landscapes; soft, melodic piano chords; and humans gathering around one another to learn and share, the film make us feel uncommonly relaxed and welcome.

Nomadland is an absolutely brutal piece of cinema. The main character Fern travels around living in a van and works from place to place with her main company being her fellow ‘nomads'. Not only is Fern contending with the daily struggles of living in a van and finding work, but she also struggles with sorrow and regret and clings to the past. What makes this movie hard to watch is that Fern doesn't compromise even when she is presented with an easy way out of her predicament. She stays true to herself and she doesn't make excuses or wallow in self-pity and she takes whatever life throws at her on the chin. She moves from one task to the next and relishes every free moment that is available to be herself. The movie presents modern work for the working class in an unflattering way as industrial, dehumanizing, menial and undignified, but it also doesn't let the nomads off the hook. The nomads might proclaim to choose their ‘free' lifestyle, but it's clear that nomads represent the most vulnerable members of modern society that are adrift with no social or economic moorings. The nomads might be more immersed in nature, but nature only presents them with peace and a temporary connection. It doesn't solve loneliness or preserve their legacy or memories. The movie is relentless in its pace and the nomadic journey is presented as one that is not just pioneering, but also as one that is escaping from something. Characters are haunted by economic realities, past memories, past family relationships and fading health. The nomads live an unpredictable life with uncertainty as their constant companion. The true bleakness of the movie comes from the contrast between the people living stable economic lives and the nomads. Monotonous and meaningless work environments devoid of human experiences such as laughter, singing, dancing, learning and experiencing nature is contrasted with pooping in a bucket in a van. The confined and limited possibilities of modern suburbia is contrasted with living in a cramped cold space eating canned food day in and day out. The movie doesn't point fingers at the economic causes or take a stance on the merits of the characters' circumstances or decisions. The true nature of one's own purgatory is left up to the viewer to decide. For Fern there is only the final realization that she derives some contentment from waking up to a horizon of possibility.

Nomadland is the right movie for the right movie. It comes at a time when the social-political backdrop features talk of universal basic income and raising the minimum wage to $15/hr. Nomadland, to a certain extent, shows what happens when people slip through the cracks of American safety net, or least what there is of it. 

The movie is not-plot driven, rather Vern (Frances McDormand) is a vessel in which we experience the life of a modern nomad. As viewers, we are guided through difference highs and lows, though primarily the latter. Her journey is a cutting reminder that there's no amount of pulling yourself up by your bootstraps that can help in certain situations. 

While Nomadland lacks dramatic or tense moments, it's not to stay there isn't thought and craftsmanship put into this film. The documentary-style adds a layer of seemingly-genuine appeal to the characters that humanizes them. The use of the circle metaphor is also well note.

Fern (Frances McDormand) finds herself out of work when the sole industry in Empire, Nevada, closes down. She outfits a van and hits the road, traveling around the Western United States. She takes on various jobs, including seasonal (Christmas) work in Amazon warehouses, restaurants, and as a park caretaker; she is too young to retire and is not ready to stop working. She meets other nomads along the way, most of whom are not trained actors and actual people who are on the road for a variety of reasons. I loved the movie. McDormand is amazing; she disappears into her character, and if you didn't know, you would think she was actually a "nomader" as well; she captures so well the internal restlessness that propels Fern and keeps her moving and alive. What I really liked about her performance, and this probably has as much to do with the choices of the director, is that McDormand is at once giving an amazing acting performance and being something of an anthropologist. Her "fictionalized" character is eliciting some honest and sometimes striking dialog from the real-life characters she is engaging with. There is something about this, at least for me, that elevates her craft as a supreme actress. Through her interactions with Linda, Swankie, Bob, and the young kid (I cannot recall his name) she meets, we not only learn more about what drives Fern, but we also learn a lot about the people who are in this lifestyle, many of them driven to the road as a result of the Great Recession. The cinematography, of course, is beautiful with all of those great panoramic shots of the American west, and the score is absolutely beautiful. The Director, Chloe Zhao, has a way of capturing the heart and mood of change in her films, and she does it brilliantly here as well. There was only one aspect of the film, which I won't mention, that I found distracted from the stream of consciousness of the film. Big thumbs up from me for a great film with great performances and immense beauty, visually and in the other people living on the road. If you like this, watch her previous film, "The Rider", which I think is the better film of the two.

Houseless, not homeless.  So this is about a woman (Frances McDormand) who has chosen to live her life on the road.  Her residence is her van, and she travels the country from odd job to odd job.  This is her story.  Now, as somebody who closely tracks movies during award season, this was on my radar.  It has been available for streaming on Hulu for a while now, but I didn't have a burning desire to watch it.  My sense of obligation took over the night before Oscar nominations dropped, and as I compose this rough draft, I am all but certain that this is a lock to be a Best Picture nominee on Monday (which it has now been named).  So how did I end up liking it?  Well, Nomadland is a well-made movie, but I can't say that it is one of my favorites.  Now I know that some people will love this movie, and I don't have any qualms with you.  There is plenty to recommend about this, and I would label this a quality film.  That said, it is not a movie that I would typically go for, and I did have difficulties connecting with this on an emotional level.  Nomadland is a very slice-of-life narrative, and the story is about bare-bones as they come.  That's not to say that this is boring, mind you.  This isn't a Terrence Malick production where nothing is happening slowly while a protagonist waxes whispered voiceover poetry.  I was always engaged with the presentation of this lifestyle, which ends up being the most compelling angle presented.  This is a life of solitude, and while there are people who live this lifestyle with a partner, most do it alone, at least according to this storyteller.  Another successful approach taken here is that they show both sides of the coin just like Trainspotting did with heroin.  They do manage to capture how choosing to live this way would be liberating from a freedom standpoint, but at the same time, they also show how there are also problems that could easily be fatal if a couple of variables turn sour.  Nomadland is a fine film that I am probably never going to watch again.  I did appreciate how genuine it felt, and other than Frances McDormand and David Strathairn, I feel like everybody else featured in this was just everyday non-acting people.  McDormand is always a pleasure to watch, and she is a large part of why this movie is as effective as it is.  I can give this a low recommendation, more so if you gravitate towards quieter and more contemplative stories.

At a pivotal point in history, when we all have the ability to discover a new appreciation for living our everyday lives, "Nomadland" helps drive that message home. The fictional story of Fern (Frances McDormand) drops us off in the nonfictional, and defunct town of Empire, Nevada, as she and her dearest belongings hesitantly shift toward a new life in a "ratty" old van. Throughout Fern's journey across the West, the audience is given true, personal stories of real-life nomads, told by the actual people themselves. Oscar Nominated Director Chloe Zhao delivers an all-around beautiful film filled with gorgeous images of the American landscape; However, even more beautiful are those up-close and vulnerable moments when the real-life characters of this film tell their stories. Frances McDormand no doubt brings home another magnificent performance, but you will leave the theater in-love with characters such as: Linda-May, Bob Wells, and Swankie. While their personal stories seem to propel Fern on her fictitious journey throughout the film, you can't help but feel as though these true stories are for the audience as a reminder, and a gift, to appreciate the life we have lived, the life we are capable of living, and those we live for. Given the images of the landscape, and the extremely personal moments with the actors in this film, as well as a short runtime, I highly suggest you see this one in theaters.

This movie seems in many ways to be so simple, pure, and quiet, but  it is also layered and complex. Some people may be bothered by not being left with a takeaway message that fits their preconceived notions.   Fern, the main character, travels in her van across western America, making a living by working mainly seasonal jobs and living in areas designated for other nomads like her in vans or RVs.  These individuals form their own community helping each other with survival skills and often meeting up on destinations on the road. This movie is not just about how the American economy can be unjust, but there is some of that. The people who are the nomads living on wheels and moving from job to job are where they are at for complex reasons; some dealing with job losses, some with having their own life struggles, some may have trouble settling in one place either because of a need for adventure or even grief that makes it too painful to stay still in one place, and some may just be a bit too eccentric for a conventional life. Or, maybe for many of these individuals there are a combination of these reasons that brings them live among a moving community of people.  Some viewers just looking for a polemic on the cruelty of capitalism have been troubled that some of these people seem to be making a choice about how they live. Others have oddly expressed the opposite, that the movie is too much of a pity part for down trodden people.   However, Zhao has wisely chosen not to use the movie to lecture or preach and has avoided making he movie seem like a political statement. Like life, the people and the choices they make do not fall into clear pigeonholes. The result is a movie that leaves us thinking about more than the economic  downturn of 2008, but about what it means to be human.

I found Chloé Zhao's sophomore effort, The Rider, a truly poignant authentic and honest portrait of its hero and I was amazed by how its cinematography draws us very close to him in the personal moments not only with its effective close-ups but also by reflecting our main character's feel of emptiness and loss in the gloomy atmosphere that prevails the entire film. However, I honestly struggled to finally get to its brilliant tear-jerking ending, simply because of its deliberate pace that never picks up even when the story demands that. Here, things are evidently different. No doubt Nomadland is a very slow-paced movie, but it has a perfect tone and the movie, consequently, rarely, if ever, drags.

A further testament of Chloé Zhao's remarkable artistic maturity, and what I genuinely loved about Nomadland, is the staggering balance it strikes between between everything it tackles from its major themes and main concepts to its minor underling details. Most notably between offering a social commentary that's relevant in the present economic environment and weavering an intricate realistic portrait of the downtrodden, underdogs, forgotten and lost individuals with an almost complete disregard to focusing on a specific social strata.

By embracing realism and detaching it from all its oft-affiliated cinematic clichés, Zhao has also managed to walk a tightrope between depicting the "Nomads" life as a salvation for our Fern and her likes and the representing this new lifestyle as a total failure that resulted from a desperate search for belongness. It's true that we see Fern striving to adapt to this new life style with all its rigors and hardships while overcoming her grief in the process, but it's evident that she "belongs" to nature because that's only where she can get the feel of freedom. We see that her conversations with other broken-hearted people alleviate their pain in the sense of "life goes on, anyway", but we barely see them offering a consoling arm around each others' shoulders.

Nomadland is poetic achievement that blurs the line between fiction and non-fiction by representing a marginalized people whom we very much recognise but also by making its titular land a realistic fictional haven for people who find their identity by letting their souls roam in the spacious wilderness, all that while serving as a tribute to the travel lovers by merely capturing the ethos of wanderlust.

However, it is 1) an absolutely incredible film 2) directed by Chloé Zhao, who not only was a finalist for directed Marvel's BLACK WIDOW, but IS the director of next November's ETERNALS, Marvel's bonkers cosmic film.

NOMADLAND is based on the nonfiction book Nomadland: Surviving America in the Twenty-First Century, and is produced/stars Frances McDormand (one of the few actors to win the "triple crown" of acting awards: (2) Oscars, (2) Prime-time Emmys, and a Tony).  The film is about MdDormand's character, Fern, who's lost her job when a mining company went out of business (this happened in real life), devastating and entire town's population; she also lost her husband, and decided to sell all of her things and hit the road: at first to search for work, but then to search for...something else - something maybe even she can't quite articulate, but that innate sense of belonging or purpose or wonder that we're all searching for to some degree.  She works at an Amazon fulfillment warehouse for awhile and meets a woman, Linda, who is also somewhat of a nomad: someone who travels around because they can and encourages Fern to head to the deserts of AZ to join a nomad community.  After trying in vain to find work, she hops in her van and does indeed head to AZ.

The rest of the film mixes beautiful widescreen shots of American landscape with real life American nomads.  Zhao (who also wrote the adapted screenplay and edited the film) does a nice job of weaving real life nomads, who likely have a FAR better sense of the life than the rest of us, with fictional stories; the nomads play fictionalized versions of themselves.  For example, Fern meets up with and befriends real life nomad Swankie while staying in a commune where leader Bob Wells (another real life nomad) informs passersby how to survive, accomplish tasks from the road, and is really a support system for fellow nomads.  It's a fascinating way of life that feels like a sequel of sorts to another real life story, INTO THE WILD, about an intelligent, young college grad who instead of going to law school gives everything away to be a nomad (that story ends tragically, as the naive youngin heads into the Alaskan interior Forrests ill prepared and died).

But here's the kicker: Fern is one of the younger folks living this lifestyle that's seemingly made up of mostly senior citizens.  The film does not paint a picture of desperate Americans who had not other choice, but instead kind of rides the line between, "yeah these people are not coming from lives of wealth or privilege" and "these people are making the conscious life to live 'free' instead of be tethered to a mortgage and career."  That is incredibly outside of my life and so I was fascinated by this seemingly bizarro lifestyle.  At one point, Fern sees a former student (she spent some time before the movie begins as a substitute teacher) who asks Fern if it's true she's homeless, to which Fern replies, "no, I'm not homeless, I'm just houseless: it's not the same thing, right?"  McDormand is incredible in a truly understated role: she brings such weight to her character without being too over dramatic or 'showy' in a wonderfully subtle performance.  You always get the feeling that there is hurt, or pain behind her eyes, but she's either too stubborn to let anyone in or she's strong enough to keep forging ahead to her next journey.  She never feels like she's desperate in her situation (like, for example, some parts of ERIN BROCKOVICH), or even like her life is spinning wildly out of her control.  Her life is merely just what it is and she's doing her thing.  There are times when Fern is offered long-term (and sometimes short-term) housing and she refuses.  Her friends around her come and go, just as they would in a true nomadic lifestyle, and sometimes that registers with her but often it doesn't.  There's no WAY she won't get at least nominated for Best Actress. and she'll likely be the first actress to be nominated for an Acting prize as well as for Best Picture as a producer.  I've read that she spent significant time living in 'her' van, and doing the jobs her Fern does on screen (though she half-jokes she stopped doing that after a bit, because "it's better for me to act like I'm exhausted all the time rather than to actually be exhausted all the time").  There are dialogue scenes of fellow (real life) nomads talking to Fern about their lives (one is riddled with cancer with a short life expectancy but decides she'd rather make good memories on the road rather than be bed-ridden in a hospital to finish her life) that are confidently shot holding on the storyteller's face for (relatively) ling takes: especially impressive when remembering a lot of these stories are from non-actors.

This film feels like it 'coincidentally' captured the entire essence of the 2020 pandemic lock-downs: the essence of what is the most difficult year in almost all of our lives.  I've been fortunate throughout this pandemic (so far  :-X ) where my wife and I have to lost our jobs (I lost a bit of pay, but nothing I would complain about) and our families have maintained good health.  But I suspect this movie will play very different for folks who've lost their jobs, or have had to live with substantial uncertainty.  I sincerely wish I could've seen this film _before_ this winter, even before the summer, to feel how this film would play under more normal circumstances.  In a world where we've all had to 'pivot' and radically shift how we approach our daily lives, NOMADLAND features the widow who eludes the loneliness of growing old in rural America by reinventing her relationship to it.  In a world where we all had to change our lives on a dime, a film about a woman who also radically changes her point of view was sobering for me to watch: impossible not to correlate with our 2020 world.  The film centers its perspective on Fern.  In doing so, the movie settles into a fascinating window into the psychological hurdles of 2020 (and, if we're being honest, 2021 which may indeed get far worse before things get better).

This is a truly beautiful character study that doesn't exactly have a traditional plot/story.  Unlike writer/director Zhao's previous (great) film THE RIDER (featuring all Native Americans, about a rodeo rider from a struggling family who has suffered a significant setback after a performance ended in brain trauma), which kind of/sort of has a resolute ending, NOMADLAND is more a snapshot of Fern's life on the road: neither a happy nor particularly sad one, merely a sobering one that feels incredibly real.  The film looks great, with lots of beautiful shots of the landscape (and some nice color contrast between the cold town Fern comes from and the dusty warm AZ deserts as well as mellowish CA).  If you liked Sean Penn's INTO THE WILD, think of this film as a spiritual sequel: like, if we took that film's hippie couple from Northern CA (Jan Burres and Rainey, played by Catherine Keener & Brian H. Dierker) and followed them around instead of the college grad.  This is maybe the best film I saw from 2020 and will almost certainly be talked about during Oscar and Golden Globe time

What I loved most about this movie I suspect may be precisely be what some others may despise about this movie. To me, its greatest strength is in its ability skillfully and respectfully to evoke "catharsis," arousal of pity and fear, in the viewer--leading to a sense of existential relief. Catharsis here is achieved by way of startlingly beautiful and bleak scenery, poetic cinematography, naturalistic acting, unhurried deliberately stressless pace (to some, perhaps interpreted as "slow" and to some, painfully slow), and ubiquitous ambiguity and lack of judgment, of any kind--thereby eshewing every possible oversimplification or false dichotomy: black/white, good/evil, funny/sad, happy/angry, brave/cowardly, weak/strong, pathetic/heroic, which encourages and allows an empathetic audience to relate more deeply not only to the story on the screen but beyond that to other complex circumstances, experiences, people in the world. (All of which is in stark contrast to the largely facile, cartoonish, dumbed-down, manipulating qualities that tend to dominate current popular movies, culture, art, and political rhetoric----and through that fundamental denial of the complexity of reality and the human condition leads to the opposite of catharsis--lack of empathy, strife, hasty and rigid judgments, undeserved self-adulation, reviling and vilification of the Other.) Although it is difficult at times (for me personally, being a single woman without a huge stockpile of retirement funds and Frances MacDormand's character being only maybe a decade older than I, at times I was gripped with panic about the future), watching Nomadland is like savoring a sublime meal prepared by a superb chef vs. the standard fare superhero or action flick being a trip to Arby's. Docked 1/2 star because--despite astonishingly subtle realism--in truth, many of the people who would or do chose to be "nomads" would be a lot more fringe and/or disturbed and/or desperate, criminal, addicted, grimy, mentally ill, troubled, unhealthy, hygiene-challenged, lost souls than the many dozens of simple, gentle, calm, balanced free-spirited characters depicted here.

Poetic, sad, joyful, meditative, and ever so beautiful. Nomandland may give Frances Mcdormand a third Oscar, and deservedly so. She gives one of them seemingly effortless performances that only actors of her caliber can pull off. A woman of a few words with a hard shell around her, yet people are pulled toward her because she is a good caring person who leaves a positive impact on everyone she meets. Nomandland weaves the story of Fern a grieving widow who finds herself houseless with little to show for after years of hardwork with the fellow nomads, each with their own story. The film gives you a glimpse on the lifestyle of a section of society that's not talked about much. These people who travel from a place to place looking for jobs and opportunities sometimes by choice and sometimes because they are out of options. The gorgeous cinematography demonstrates how beautiful the nature in all the many places they visit and makes a case for why one might be tempted to be around all this beauty all day every day, but then it reminds you how harsh nature can be as well when one under the mercy of the elements. This lifestyle is hard, very hard, but it also offers its people a chance to see new places, make new friends, and live many adventures, so when Fern (more than once) was afforded to opt out and settle with people who love her and care for her, she still chose the independence and freedom given to her by being a nomad. I would not have made the same choice (I value running water in toilets way too much), but I adore her for sticking to her guns. Kudos to Chloé Zhao's patient storytelling that blends Frances Mcdormand's performance with mostly unprofessional cast of people seemlessly. She did it before in The Rider, and she struck gold yet again here. Ludovico Einaudi score is so haunting and majestic, I really want these piano chords in my life for a long time. Loved this film and I highly recommend it.

If you're looking for an overt criticism of American material culture and the shortcomings of capitalism in the manner of Grapes of Wrath, told through very prominent depictions of fruit rotting in orchards and private security breaking up government settlements, you won't find it here. Instead, Zhao uses sweeping landscapes, emotional moments, incredible cinematography, and a single focal protagonist to discuss both economic and personal struggle rather than a single lone theme. Fern is driven to the nomad lifestyle by a combination of economic change and personal loss, finding along the way both a sense of jarring discomfort in the practical difficulty associated with a mobile lifestyle (along with mild annoyance to bristling disgust from those from many of those people who live more conventionally), but also an unorthodox camraderie in her transient companions that often share similar motivations and a sense of liberation in her lack of ties. What begins as an economic necessity gradually becomes a somewhat self-medicating isolation, as Fern is presented with opportunities to heal from her husband's death and return to sedentary life, but finding it near-impossible to do so. Some may expect the film to be a pure critique of materialism (and commentaries on superficial comforts and needless consumption are certainly present), but to present Fern as some sort of enlightened and perfectly content tramp would have been a far cheaper experience than the complex character study that we actually received. People who resort to such a lifestyle are real people, each with distinctive experiences and histories, and that is a critical intention of Zhao's narrative. McDormand is electric - spontaneous and sincere, one of her all-time great performances, and it would be no surprise if she ends up with another Best Actress for her shelf when the postponed Oscars roll around. Seeing an opening scene with her by a frigid Midwestern wire fence has to be a Fargo homage, right? (4/5)

​There is no easy way to describe a movie about a woman who chooses to become a self-sufficient person of both strength and courage while living a lifestyle few would find either desirable or even possible. Accept the fact that the talents and persona of a Frances McDormand are so unique that quite possibly - no other woman could bring this character to the big screen. The movie is adapted from the 2017 Non-Fiction book title  Nomadland: Surviving America in the Twenty First Century. It is the story of a woman whose entire life first comes to a personal and economic halt during the financial crisis of 2008. Her long-time husband and life partner dies. The plant that they both worked in for many years closes. The town that they lived in literally becomes a ghost town. Faced with little monies, a home that will be lost to the bank and no immediate prospects for employment, our central character "FERN by name" takes to the road in her van. The van becomes her answer to those that inquire about her lifestyle as one of being Houseless but not Homeless. Her van becomes her mobile Conestoga Wagon that allows her the freedom to join an ever-expanding group of similar circumstanced seniors who have fallen on hard economic times and become self-styled NOMADS traveling from campsite to campsite to find parttime jobs wherever they might be. This movie becomes a travelogue of the American West as Fern Works as a queen of all trades in a campground in South Dakota, a harvester of Beets in Nebraska, a general employee in an Amazon fulfillment center in Arizona and an ever-expanding list of jobs that provide the monies necessary to survival. This is a story of community, of self-preservation and of emotional and personal search for what will become the rest of her life.  This is also the story of people whose lives have become that of Nomad, Traveler, Gypsie or Bedouin - whose genesis was that of a dessert dweller. As you enter the theater you might choose to ask yourself: Is the credibility and strength of performance significant enough to define your sense of entertainment or enjoyment?
Rating: A - U - F - P = A Unique Female Performance

Chloé Zhao's "Nomadland" is a poetic, thought-provoking and soulful drama that sheds light on the little-known lives of modern-day nomads. With her third feature, writer/director Chloé Zhao has crafted a compassionate portrait of a marginalized community on the fringes of society. It's the filmmaker's first attempt to humanize struggles faced by modern-day nomads in the U.S., but she pulls it off seamlessly. Using captivating cinematography, Zhao draws viewers into the world of a widowed woman that embarks on a journey through the American West. Zhao's decision to shoot the film during the magic-hour of the day is risky, but it works immensely. It lends a sense of intimacy and authenticity to the movie that is missing from most neorealist dramas. Zhao's screenplay is also superb, and effectively uses minimal dialogue to convey the grief experienced by the nomad community. It is hard to not praise the phenomenal performances from the cast. Frances McDormand delivers one of the finest performances of her career as Fern. With thoughtful expressions, she conveys the grief, loneliness and resilience of a woman that refuses to conform towards standard ways of living in society. The supporting cast is outstanding and also worthy of attention. Zhao's decision to cast non-professional real-life nomads in supporting roles pays of tremendously. Although "Nomadland" is undeniably an unforgettable drama, ultimately it is not a flawless film. If there's a minor drawback to the movie, it moves at a meandering pace that tests the viewer's patience. Moreover, it's portrayal of a niche subculture may not appeal towards mainstream audiences. Nonetheless, fans of Chloé Zhao's previous films will definitely enjoy "Nomadland" and so will movie-goers seeking meaningful entertainment. At a time when nomadic living remains a little-known subculture, one only hopes that it will evoke empathy for marginalized communities whose lives are all too rarely seen in Cinema.

Nomadland opens with text explaining that after 80 years the gypsum mine in Empire, Nevada closed and the town quickly ceased to exist. Fern, a 60ish former resident of Empire, now travels the American West living out of her modified van moving from town to town, campsite to campsite, taking odd jobs here and there. Frances McDormand gives a wonderful performance as Fern. She is far more understated than her characters in Fargo, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, or even Almost Famous, but, no matter how broad or intimate the role, her great talent as an actress is to make any character that she plays feel very real. It is no surprise that McDormand has earned a Best Actress Oscar nomination for her work here. There is a wistful, bittersweetness to Fern and her nomadic lifestyle and also to the movie itself.

As both writer (adapting Jessica Bruder's nonfiction book of the same name) and director, Chloe Zhao gives her film the look and feel of a documentary. This approach helps Nomadland in some ways and hurts it in others. It will come as no surprise that many of the fellow travelers and nomads Fern encounters and befriends are real life nomads. They do a fine job in their scenes with a two-time Academy Award winner because the movie only requires them to be themselves. A gathering of nomads in Arizona where they trade stories, supplies, and tips and advice for living on the road is the most interesting segment of the film. That scene along with the scenes of the real people sharing their stories and insights made part of me wish that Zhao had made a documentary instead of a dramatization.

Seeing the beautifully photographed landscapes of the American West from the Nevada desert to Arizona to the Dakota badlands is a treat. The Oscar nominated cinematography by Joshua James Richards captures the quiet, enchanting beauty in what seems like a desolate landscape. 

Many scenes in Nomadland are short, giving us only snippets of the lives Fern encounters and her own life as well. David Strathairn has a small but great performance as a fellow wanderer debating if he should settle down again. Their scenes together are touching moments and we want them to last and hope they meet each other again. We get a brief scene of Fern visiting her sister and an argument about the real estate market begins to brew but stops short. She moves from place to place so the film cannot help feeling episodic but it is still well-paced. Nomadland is about a wanderer, but it is never aimless. 

There is not much that feels contrived in Nomadland but at a certain point I knew what would happen in the final scene. We spend a lot of quiet moments with Fern but we also feel kept at a distance from her, not unlike the distance she keeps from those that try to get close to her. We begin the film thinking that her life as a nomad is purely out of necessity but then it seems it is by choice. Perhaps the real answer for Fern and the real life nomads is somewhere in between. Nomadland is worth watching for the glimpse at this quasi-off-the-grid lifestyle but to learn more about it I suppose I will have to read the book.

It is not a credible choice for those who were raised and lived comfortable lives in the middle classes to set out, once again, in nothing but an old converted van and a few carefully chosen possessions.  Working in Amazon fulfillment centers is much tougher than portrayed.  Anyone choosing such a life past  70 years old is desperate and/or neigh onto delusional.  The benefits of the communal life,  where everyone "sees each other again other down the road", bolstered by the kumbaya of campfire singalongs is a nice way for those who can afford the movie to create a pretty-ribbon-box-image for what are actually thrown away lives of silent destitution.

I thought this movie really did a great job of showing us the pros and cons of such a life without wallowing in any sort of pity. Never really a moment where Fern was doomed or without resources. She struggled but was never threatened or left without the ability to go on. I thought that was nice, to not make this about one extremely sad story but more about the idea of nomadic people in modern day society as a whole. This movie is about Fern, but through her we see so many more stories. Some about people who wanted the freedom, some about people who were forced into a more economic lifestyle, some who didn't want to spend their lives punching a clock.

We see Fern's ability to live this life in everything she does. How easily she walks away from the dog and from every opportunity to put down roots, how proud she is of her van which she always personifies. This movie becomes less about an economic recession and more about a way of life that is in no way lacking or unproud, despite how the rest of society sees it. And yet, we are constantly reminded that it is an economic depression that put some people in this lifestyle. We see how seasonal workers move across the country looking for gigs, Amazon paying for trailer park spots for them and in a way acknowledging that they aren't paying someone enough to live "The American dream".

It's both a sad and beautiful film. But it's not sad in the sense that it feels hopeless or pathetic. It's sad in a sense that these people have to give up so much for their freedom. Their life seems almost envious to us as we watch them travel and see the sights and be fully independent, yet the movie shows us the small sacrifices like not being able to eat dinner and be vulnerable without someone walking up and peering in your window or having the luxury of starting a family.

Home is somewhere that we feel comfortable in it and somewhere that people we love are around. It describes the spiritual values ​​in life very well. Without them, we don't feel like we are at home, even we have a shelter to protect and a bed to sleep in. When we do not have a place to call home, then we seek help which Fern did later on in the movie. I also did like how the film tries to point out other problems, such as suicide. However, it was a bit pale.

Now let's talk about the things that made me upset about this movie. As I said, the first hour of the film was excellent. But I really did not want to continue watching it after that one hour. I feel like that because pretty much nothing happens after. We see Fern staying with other people and switching jobs, but nothing much really changes for her while doing all these. The main change in the story was after everyone left and she got alone, but there was nothing more, and the film just kept on going the same for an hour. At those moments, it also tries to be emotional, but I think it couldn't really manage it, and those moments felt a bit exaggerated. There were also some weird scenes that I did not understand why they were even in the film, and it made me feel a bit uncomfortable.

To conclude, I liked the first half of the movie, which reminded me of Into the Wild. However, I'd have been much happier at the end of the film if it did not take too long. It has really great messages, but I think it couldn't manage to be a film that drags you along. The last half determines my feelings about this film, and it is not that good. Chloe Zhao's third feature film is part travelogue, part documentary, part social-political statement, and rightfully an early Oscar frontrunner. Based on Jessica Bruder's book, it provides us with an insight into a lesser-known section of the US population who survives by living like modern nomads, travelling around the country picking up jobs in farms, parks and even Amazon as migrant workers. Juxtaposing the bleak but majestic American landscapes captured by cinematographer Joshua James Richards with the stark personal and/or socio-economic conditions that drive them into this lifestyle, this minimalistic film beautifully and perfectly conveys the resilience and nobility of these people's stripped down and simple lives. Blurring the line between fact and fiction, it begins with a fictional character from a real place that's very much a sign of the times: Frances McDormand's Fern, a widow from Empire, Nevada who is now on the road after her hometown vanished off the map due to the closure of its local mining industry. However, the people she interacts and meets on the road (bar David Strathairn's Dave) are played by non-professionals who are actually part of the nomad community, each with their own (true) story to tell; which this film does, succinctly and elegantly. Playing a character not unlike Mildred in Three Billboards... with an occasional slip into Marge Gunderson, it's no stretch for the two-time Oscar winner but it's the way she blends seamlessly into the actual communities that will almost ensure another nomination. Arguably, it does romanticize this way of living and perhaps paints it rosier than it really is, but with Zhao's very deliberate decision to avoid overblown melodramatics, the end result is an articulate, defiant and empowering film that stays with you as Ludovico Einaudi's haunting piano score sends you off to the comforts of your own home.

When asked what my favorite movie genre is, I like to say I'm about any as long as a film is good. I'll just be blunt: Nomadland wasn't for me. It's all in the name: the film journeys through people and places at a reflective and lackadaisically free-flowing pace, writer/director Chloé Zhao once again observing an overlooked piece of America with her unique lens of care and compassion.

Taking inspiration from Jessica Bruder's memoir Nomadland: Surviving America in the Twenty-First Century, Frances McDormand plays Fern, a woman who sells her home and possessions to live and travel through the United States in a van after her small mining town totally vacates when its main production plant shuts down. As with Zhao's previous works, the film is populated with non-actors aside from its lead character and several others, but you'd never know it given the director's ability to get seamless performances out of her cast.

But that same naturalistic approach is what closed me off from the film. For all of its undeniable merits, I just couldn't connect to Nomadland. It takes its time intimately bouncing between people's stories and the outskirts of America's environments, showcasing it all with an almost melancholic pang of beauty. There's just no bigger picture, and I couldn't extract any personal value from this very vérité style as a result. Still, I'm sure others will.

A few days ago I watched the Academy Awards ceremony and, to be honest, I have not seen any of the nominated films until today. That is why I am going write about the winner to Best Motion Picture of the Year "Nomadland".

In visual, auditory and technical terms is a piece of art. It has Extreme Wide shots which show as the incredible pureness of nature combined at the perfection with subtle beautiful Close-Up shots to emphasize on the facial expressions of the marvelous Frances McDormand who, in order to focus more on her role and be more realistic, had been sleeping in a van during the cast; a perfect soundtrack that fits with the images and the color palette, composed by the great Ludovico Einaudi; and many professional filming techniques by Joshua James Richards.
The story began with Fern, a resident of Empire, Nevada, who decides to leave her hometown when her husband dies. The plots moves on talking about these "nomads" who live in vans moving between towns and small villages where they stay during some days or even weeks. I really liked when Fern said "I'm not homeless, I'm just houseless" referring to her new lifestyle and the critic point of view about the capitalism; Zhao covers well the issue of poverty and the unfair pension for retirees from the state to old people who just want to work for not living beyond their means. It is remarkable the arc of the character and how the protagonist evolves as the movie progresses, but not all the merit goes to Chloé: many actors and actresses as Bob Welles, Charlene Swankie and Linda May play as themselves and talk about their experiences or problems in real life, so it is like a documentary more than a movie. 
In spite of this little inconvenient for me, the rest of the film is perfect if you like true stories and want to learn about the lifestyle of those who our economic system has abandoned. I personally recommended as a Spanish sixteen years old teenager who really likes cinema.

I was presented with this movie with no premise or introduction, and I found that it wasn't filled with boring, trite Disney tropes, one of its most compelling features.  It was an absolute joy to watch fiction I couldn't predict and sleep through - ho-hum, yeah, someone offered her a dog, so that's going to be the hook, the Heartwarming Saving Grace for her life.  The dog, the jobs, the lottery sign, the knocking man, the peeing man, the Knight in Shining Armor, the contrary sister, the dying friend, the return to familiar ground, Fern's appearance, even the nomadic community itself;  after a while I found myself looking for deflated cliches like they were Easter eggs. Many commonplace Dramatic plot-wheel points were presented and then quietly left to die, just like real life will do.  LOVED. THAT. 
If I have one disappointment, the movie didn't end with an acknowledgment that it's possible to live like this and have internal happiness. I don't mean that stumbling into abject poverty, loss, or unstable living situation is pleasant or desirable, ever, I mean that *emotionally speaking*, not everyone wants or needs the assumed brass rings of intimate personal relationships or entirely predictable life, some people find their peace in a different place.  To me, once Fern healed from her grief and losses, she seemed to be made for life alone on the road; it was acknowledged that she was always 'weird,' 'adventurous,' and generally somewhat unlike other people.  It would have been a wonderful character arc. Frances McDormand did a fantastic job of portraying a person with odd but kind personal skills and yet extreme boundaries, and a lot of wisdom, resilience, pain, and sorrow,  but Fern's eventual good fit for the life she chose seemed lost in projected expectations (by the writers/directors) of what she "ought to" want. It's the one truism they didn't disassemble.  
Unfortunately, by the end, Fern still seemed pretty much the same sad, exhausted, and emotionally grim person we first met, as if the best anyone could hope for from nomadic life is buried anxiety and tolerated suffering. Moving her from stunted and stoic grief to inner peace that had the eventual potential to blossom into inner joy would have been satisfying.  A hint of a smile and an ending score that evolved slightly from sounding like it was mourning humanity's existence itself would have been enough, just a brief and relatively ambiguous suggestion of the possibility.
I don't seek a "happy Disney ending," and this one was wryly satisfying as the ultimate deflated cliche. Still, when it's portrayed at all, the nomadic existence is usually presented as being a frightening, filthy, hopeless, lonely, incompetent, and terrible life, panhandling its way to bare survival, maintained due to addiction, mental illness, pathological misanthropy, or perhaps unrequited stupidity. The nomad community refuted this joyously; Bob Wells was marvelous. Of course, all of those things do have the potential to be true. Still, since we were following Fern, it would have been satisfying to have the flip side portrayed by her personally: that even if it's not an intentional goal, a single nomadic living situation can be a positive and even transcendent alternative to the right individual.
