It's commendable that a Chinese national, Zhao Ting can so perfectly create such a poignant testament to the trailer nomads of the USA. The way she paces and edits her own work is a joy to the eye – there's poetry in each sequence of her film. This is also attributable to the outstanding work of her director of photography; Joshua James Richard - his stylish use of a camera with strong, steady images, is nothing less than superb.  Zhao also balances her use of music to its most evocative form, and features inspired use of the ambiance compositions by Italian Ludovico Einaudi, from his ‘7 Days Walking' sessions. Her images, with his music blend in perfect harmony, creating many high points throughout this engaging picture.  

In this case, it's good to see Frances McDormand away from her now predictable, overly dark Cohen Bros works, and some other over-ripe roles we've seen.  She's perfect as the somewhat lost soul, living with her memories and finding it difficult to allow herself to become too close, even when some offer her the comfort of a bonding relationship.  McDormand's nude scene added nothing to the story (they rarely do) but was at least tastefully done, but that said...how many places will there be in this dry desert landscape, where you can find an Oasis that no one else seems to know about, and you can swim naked, without fear of leeches, snakes, and ‘human' predators? Might this seemingly romanticized scene possibly have been shot in some hotel or a closed studio set, and likely added as an adult rating grab?   

Slipping co-star David Strathairn in amongst other roadies works quite nicely, and he's a welcome addition to this work. I realize it takes all kinds to make a world, still, when this obviously lonely woman gives up the offer of a loving home life, to go back to all the desperately looming problems yet to be experienced on the road – might be  a rather long bow to draw (?)
  
Taken overall, Nomadland is one of the few recent movies to earn its nominations and awards (despite the absence of over-the-top action and effects) simply for its heart and soul. It sort of seems a pity Zhao has been wooed by the big-time, with a blockbuster Marvel Comic slated to be her next - It's to be hoped we may see more of her doco-like humane work. Also, how foolish is China to censor one of its higher achieving citizens - because she's been critical of some aspects of China's policies – their loss, our gain.

After stowing away her material possessions and hitting the highway, a widowed van-dweller roams the seasonal workplaces and temporary sanctuaries of the transient life. It's a lonesome road, one of fleeting connections and uncertain destinations; a solitary existence that's half choice and half necessity. I've noticed a certain sense of daydreamy romanticism floating around this sort of lifestyle recently, the glamorized prospect of working from a cel signal with the great outdoors as a backdrop, but Nomadland strips away much of that veneer in showing the other side of the coin. There's promise in such freedom, but also great risk, and not every van lifer is cut out for the harsh realities of such a compartmentalized existence.

Frances McDormand drew a best actress Oscar for her portrayal of Fern, the wandering protagonist whose compassion leads her to make deep connections with similar spirits, but whose withdrawn emotional restlessness forces those relationships to remain decidedly brief. She's wonderful, as expected, with an expressive authenticity that can make the film feel more like a documentary than a staged drama. Evidently, moviegoers weren't the only ones taken by that convincing act: without a firm script, much of the film's dialogue is delivered by true nomads who happened into the indie-scale production and, taking McDormand for one of their own, opened up to her. That knowledge can cause the film to teeter a bit too close to exploitation, but it also lends extra credibility and sentimental power to the viewing experience.

Chloe Zhao's follow up to The Rider (2017, my first film for WFC!) is a beautiful drama with a powerhouse of a performance from Frances McDormand. After losing everything during the 2008 recession, Fern (McDormand) decides to become a 'Nomad', a fairly recent phenomenon in the US. Post the 2008 depression, many 60-70 year olds were left with not enough money to retire, but also not enough to work and maintain a home. So they took to the road, roaming the country in camper vans which become their homes, looking for seasonal work, in bars, restaurants, or in Fern's case, an enormous Amazon warehouse in Nevada. Nomadland is an early frontrunner for film of the year (As ridiculous as that sounds in January) but it really is incredible film making, capturing this way of life beautifully, led by McDormand. The people Fern meets on her travels are mostly real life Nomads, giving real authenticity to the story. Nomadland's scope is wide enough to bring you on a roaming journey that you are so invested in from the offset, you really feel all of Fern's emotions as she struggles through hardships as well as enjoying perfect moments of serenity in the silence and beauty of this way of life.
Nomadland had some interesting stretches, but as a whole was ultimately boring. I'll still be looking forward to the director's next venture.

McDormand and the director Zhao between them create so many layers of meaning in this beautifully shot exploration of loss and living, that Fern becomes a brilliant metaphor for the slow erosion of the American Dream, whilst also being a ‘pioneer', like the people who founded it. It made me think of The Decline of the West (literal translation 'The Twilight of the Evening lands') by Oswald Spengler ( I know he is frowned upon a bit nowadays) but his insights really work here; that real existence is actually in the becoming, not the 'become', and that a fixed 'civilization' is actually a stop sign at the end of the road. The road itself is the real culture here. That Fern is on the road because an ‘Empire' literally came to an end fully underlines that idea. I really loved the poetry of time sewn into the film to; the word play around rocks, dinosaurs, light years, fossils, and a perfectly placed Shakespearean sonnet. And the endless sunsets, a central metaphor I think. It could have been called 'The Evening Lands', or ‘Summer's Lease' Such a cerebral and melancholy delight, and presented in a beautiful and lucid light.

Not all movies need to be a thoroughly developed story with character arches or a mapped out plot. In fact, if Nomadland was anything like another traditional Hollywood film it's tale would ring both cliché and disingenuous.

Instead, Nomadland is a story anyone can relate to: where do you go when you have nothing left in life? Taking a setup based on the growing epidemic of homelessness in America particularly in the early 2010's following the great recession, the film focuses on Frances McDormand's Fern. Fern is an ageing woman who lives the life of a nomad, traveling and living in her van after her husband dies and the small town they share becomes all but abandoned.

The film follows what is a seemingly aimless woman among countless equally aimless folks who are all merely making their way in an aimless new way of life. Sprinkled with glints of happiness, hope as much as small tragedies-- Nomadland plays something like a documentary of one woman's travels.

It's beautifully shot, subtly acted, emotionally investing and very much worth the journey.

That's a powerful concept, "home". Fern (Frances McDormand) even corrects the idea that she isn't homeless, but "houseless". You see, Fern is a nomad who travels the American West and Great Plains, taking part-time jobs here and there and meeting other nomads here and there. Fern doesn't do this in a way to discover herself (à la Wild) or because she has become disenchanted with contemporary society (à la Into the Wild), Fern does this out of necessity. She loved her home when it was a house, located at the edge of a company town in Northwest Nevada, where she lived with her beloved husband and remained after he passed away. The mineral plant closed and town with it — the zip code was deactivated shortly thereafter. Zhao shoots this film like a documentary. It's subtle, nothing is forced. Like Fern and her nomadic lifestyle, the plot never really goes where you expect it to — beginning with the dog. I was expecting to encounter nomads who were "houseless" for the more perceived reasons — drug abuse, mental illness, evading the law — but we get nothing of the sort. In fact, Fern wants to work, she "likes work," but work is scarce. It's deeply American with "salt of the Earth" feelings throughout. It feels authentic because it is authentic; except for McDormand and David Straitharn, who plays a love-interest (but remember what I noted about this meandering plot), most of the characters are themselves nomads. God, I loved Swankie (Swankie). Her little rehash of her life, why she's accepted her fate, is one of the most moving couple of minutes I've seen in a while. I'm not much of a crier, but this brought me damn close — the beginning is cut btw. (How is she not an actress?!) I also thought Fern was going to follow Swankie, I wanted Fern to follow Swankie, but that's not what we get, and that's okay. I appreciated this movie the more I let it settle in. I like movies that do that. I don't think it'd be my 2021 Best Picture, but I'd be happy if it won. Watch it.

Gorgeously shot (cinematographer Joshua James Richards does stellar work) and with yet another outstanding performance from Frances McDormand, Chloé Zhao tells the story of people who have been cast aside and forgotten; people who have given everything they have to a broken system and end up being left with nothing to show for it. But that's not all it is, it's also a character study that deals heavily with loss and letting go. ‘Nomadland' is depressing in a multitude of ways; it's like a heavy weight on your shoulders where the realistic, yet poetic quality makes it simultaneously difficult and captivating to watch. It's not easy to see these salt of the earth people suffer, struggling to scrape by and scrounging for some shred of hope wherever they can, but it's also kind of beautiful to see them find it in unexpected places and people. If one thing's for sure, it would be hard to come out the other side of this film not feeling very grateful and privileged for what and who you have in your own life.

When Roger Ebert famously spoke about cinema as a machine for creating empathy, you'd be forgiven for thinking he had this film in mind. Few films so adeptly and completely take the viewer inside the experience of a life that is alien to most of us, and enable the willing viewer to empathetically enter into the experiences portrayed on screen. It's visually stunning - America's wide-open spaces have rarely seemed so striking, and to me there especially seemed to be something about how the light is captured that is at times almost overwhelming in its beauty. Frances McDormand's performance may be the best of her remarkable career. What's especially remarkable is the lack of romanticism  - this does not glamorise a life it doesn't understand; it doesn't patronisingly canonise the poor and the marginalised; instead, it's examining the human fall pout of the Great Recession, honestly seeking to come to terms with the question of 'how then do people live' once lives have been so thoroughly upended. There is beauty and sadness in the smallest details, visual allusions that will reward repeat viewings, and the profound sense of real lives being excavated and examined. Compassionate, beautiful, and intelligent, this is may well be a quiet modern masterpiece.

Chloé Zhao's oscar-winning 'Nomadland' is a poetic, 108-minute affair that takes viewers on a cross-country journey across mid-west America. Since its debut at the 2020 Venice film festival, the film has gone on to receive a plethora of accolades, including the top prize at both the Venice Film Festival and the Toronto International Film Festival. The film also secured Chloé Zhao her first Academy Award, making her the first woman of colour to win the award and only the second female to win the coveted Oscar.

'Nomadland' tells the story of Fern (McDormand), a widowed woman in her sixties who lives in Empire, Nevada. After the local mine closes, Fern is left in the desolate town and decides to pack up her belongings and live her life as a nomad. As she adapts to her new life, she takes up various jobs; from working as an Amazon employee to an RV park host. Along the way, she meets other silver-haired nomads, Swankie, Linda-May and Dave, from various places she's travelled and learns their life stories and their philosophies.

Frances McDormand gives a sensational performance as Fern. Her portrayal of the character is utterly entrancing, and believe it or not, the only cast members who were real actors were McDormand and Strathairn. The rest of the cast were real nomads who live Fern's actual lifestyle. Despite her lack of experience, Charlene Swankie gives a poignant performance as 'Swankie', one of the friends Fern meets on her travels. She gives an incredibly moving monologue about her life and some of the things she has seen. Fern also meets Bob Wells, a man who found peace and comfort in the nomad lifestyle after dealing with personal tragedy. He leaves Fern with the idea that in the nomad community, goodbyes are never final; you'll always see each other again down the road.

Joshua James Richards provides 'Nomadland' with crisp, cool-toned cinematography and smooth camera work that compliments the film's aesthetic in such a unique way. The various wide shots help to emphasise that the life of a nomad doesn't revolve around one specific locale. Chloé Zhao gets to let her creative juices flow as she takes the director's chair for the third time. Her talent shines throughout the entire film. Viewers will see why she deserved her Oscar by the closing credits. Not only does Zhao direct 'Nomadland', but she also served as editor for the film. Zhao's editing, mixed with Richard's cinematography, creates a beautiful mixture of visuals, a real feast for the eyes.

The cast and crew got a feel for the 'nomad' lifestyle while filming as they lived in vans over the four months they shot the film. If you're a fan of Zhao, then you should consider adding her two previous films; 'Songs My Brother Taught Me' and The Rider'. But if your wanting to watch another in-depth character study, then 'The Secret Life of Walter Mitty' is one for you. You can also catch Zhao in the directors chair again with the 2021 Marvel blockbuster 'Eternals', due to be released Nov 5.

By the closing credits, viewers are left with complex ideas and simple quotes. The theme of memory and how people keep their loved ones' legacies alive after they're gone plays a part in many of the character's stories. The quote 'What's remembered lives' leave viewers with the idea that if you remember someone or something, then their memory will still live on. 'Nomadland' shows how people affected by the Great Recession had a fresh start as they moved into the ever-changing nomad lifestyle, swapping homes for vans and heating for a mountain of blankets.

Overall, Chloé Zhao delivers a poetic, emotional film that deals with complex ideas and themes. Both Zhao and McDormand are a tour de force in 'Nomadland', and their myriad of awards prove it. So if you're looking for a film that captivates you and draws you in, then 'Nomadland' is the one for you.

You get a sense of a fictional version of the nomadic lifestyle in the game "Cyberpunk 2077", and it is drawn extensively from the real-life, factual vandwelling community. Personally I wasn't even aware of their reality until I watched Chloé Zhao's "Nomadland" – a beautiful painting of a lifestyle that is minimalist, rugged, simple and peaceful in the same breath.
Frances McDormand is the perfect brush to outline and fill life into the picture. As an embedded nomad in a semi-documentary like depiction with some real life nomads going through their journeys, McDormand blends perfectly and possibly slid completely into that skin to actualize the character. Fern, a woman in her middle ages, anchored to the industrial town where she had been living and working for years with her now deceased husband, finds herself fresh out of a job and on the road to survive.
Travelling through towns to find and work jobs, she dwells in her van as a lone rider, until she comes across Linda May, who tells her more about the vandwelling community and Bob Wells, who leads and organizes camps for nomads. Fern watches, observes, absorbs what she experiences in one such camp in the Arizonian desert, finding herself a new family in that process.
Zao's Oscar winning effort at directing with Joshua James Richards' cinematography is simplistic, serene and as redundant as I may sound, like an exquisite piece of art with a really gritty and real theme at the center of it all. McDormand, who was already a two-time Oscar winner, ups her ante as Fern and bagged her thoroughly deserving third as the lead actress in this film.
David Strathairn plays a convincing supporting character in Fern's journey and deserves kudos for his portrayal as well. Along with so many real life nomads putting together a realistic picture of the lifestyle – the everyday, the togetherness, the simple humane moments that should ideally bind all of humankind – nomads or otherwise.
The film strings together so many beautiful natural quotes by all the characters, specially Swankie; but one that stays in my mind is a line that by Merle, a nomad that Fern meets in Arizona and she narrates a story about a colleague who worked all his life, and passed away just before retiring:
"..then he told me before he died, just don't waste any time, girl. Don't waste any time. So I retired as soon as I could. I didn't want my sailboat to be in the driveway when I died. So… yeah. And it's not. My sailboat is out here in the desert."
